## The Resource Management Act: Aotearoa's Planning Backbone

The Resource Management Act (RMA) 1991 is New Zealand's principal piece of environmental and planning legislation. Hailed at the time as the first comprehensive law in the world to require sustainable management of resources, it replaced roughly 80 earlier acts and orders in one sweeping reform [[1]](cite://1/1). Its architect was Sir Geoffrey Palmer, who described it as 'one of the most comprehensive reforms in the Western world' [[2]](cite://2/1).

At its core, the RMA requires all developments — with the exception of mineral extraction, which is covered separately by the Crown Minerals Act 1991 — to avoid, mitigate, or remedy adverse environmental effects [[1]](cite://1/2). Resource consents for the use of water, air, soil, and land must be obtained from the relevant regional, city, or district councils, with provision for public participation in decision-making [[1]](cite://1/3).

The act also replaced the old Town and Country Planning Act and required councils to prepare new district plans to manage land use in an environmentally sustainable way. An Environment Court replaced the Planning Tribunal [[3]](cite://3/1). Its philosophical ethos, at least initially, was 'more free market than regulatory' — as long as there was no environmental harm, people were largely free to build as they wished [[3]](cite://3/2).

### What the RMA Covers

The RMA's reach is broad. It controls land use, manages water quality, regulates air emissions, and protects coastal areas and estuaries [[4]](cite://4/1)[[5]](cite://5/1)[[6]](cite://6/1)[[7]](cite://7/1). Regional councils are responsible for monitoring these areas and issuing permits and consents accordingly [[8]](cite://8/1)[[5]](cite://5/2).

Notably, the 1991 act was a landmark moment for Māori. Prior legislation had largely ignored Māori historical, spiritual, and cultural concerns. The RMA explicitly recognised Māori spiritual and cultural values and the principles of the Treaty of Waitangi. Environmental developments required consultation with iwi (tribes), and resource consent applications had to be sent to iwi authorities [[9]](cite://9/1).

However, not everything falls under the RMA's umbrella. Biosecurity — including border protection for agriculture and forestry — is governed separately under the Biosecurity Act 1993 [[10]](cite://10/1).

### The Case for Reform

Despite its ambitions, the RMA has been criticised from multiple directions over the years. Palmer himself acknowledged it wasn't perfect: 'You can have development, or you can have sustainability. There's an inherent contradiction in this which we haven't resolved yet' [[11]](cite://11/1).

Environmental advocates have argued that successive governments failed to provide adequate policy guidance to regional councils, and that councils themselves had increasingly become 'development agencies on behalf of government', undermining the act's protective intent [[12]](cite://12/1). Parliamentary Commissioner for the Environment Jan Wright warned that proposed changes amounted to a 'Trojan horse', arguing the RMA itself provides the balance to economic imperatives and 'is not, and should not become, an economic development act' [[13]](cite://13/1).

On the other side, critics have long complained the RMA makes it too hard and too costly to build housing, infrastructure, and renewable energy. Federated Farmers called the current system 'broken', with farmers spending excessive time and money on resource consents for straightforward activities [[14]](cite://14/1).

There has been bipartisan recognition that the act has both failed to protect the environment sufficiently and wrapped projects in excessive red tape [[15]](cite://15/1).

## The Coalition Government's Reform Programme

The current National-led coalition government has pursued the most ambitious overhaul of the RMA in its history, structured in three phases.

**Phase one** involved repealing legislation introduced by the previous Labour government and making urgent early amendments, including revisions to stock exclusion rules, winter grazing, Te Mana o te Wai (the concept of water as a taonga — a treasured resource), mining consenting, and the suspension of Significant Natural Area (SNA) requirements [[16]](cite://16/1).

**Phase two** introduced a second RMA Amendment Bill focused on infrastructure, energy, housing, farming, and natural hazards, alongside the single largest package of national direction changes in New Zealand's history — seven new national direction instruments and amendments to 14 existing ones [[17]](cite://17/1). A Fast-track Approvals Bill was also introduced as a 'one-stop shop' consenting regime for significant projects [[18]](cite://18/1).

**Phase three** — the most sweeping — proposes to scrap the RMA entirely and replace it with two new laws [[19]](cite://19/1)[[15]](cite://15/2):

- A **Natural Environment Act**, focused on managing environmental effects from activities, including setting quantified environmental limits at a regional level [[15]](cite://15/3)
- A **Planning Act**, focused on enabling urban development and infrastructure [[19]](cite://19/2)

RMA Reform minister Chris Bishop said the goal is to cut administrative and compliance costs by 45 percent, grounded in the principle of 'the enjoyment of property rights' — allowing people to do more on their own land as long as it doesn't harm others [[20]](cite://20/1). The reforms also propose more standardised zoning nationally (New Zealand currently has 1,175 different zone types across its councils, compared to just 13 in Japan) and a new planning disputes tribunal for faster, lower-cost resolution of disagreements [[20]](cite://20/2)[[15]](cite://15/4).

Notably, the reforms would remove the Treaty of Waitangi clause currently in the RMA [[20]](cite://20/3).

In December 2025, the coalition formally introduced the Planning Bill and Natural Environment Bill to Parliament, with the aim of passing them before the 2026 election [[21]](cite://21/1). Labour leader Chris Hipkins indicated his party would not repeal the legislation if elected, though it would likely make amendments — suggesting the 'repeal and replace cycle' that has plagued RMA reform for decades may finally be drawing to a close [[21]](cite://21/2).

### Reactions

Responses to the reforms have been mixed. Federated Farmers welcomed the shift, saying the RMA had been 'the single biggest handbrake on growing agricultural productivity' [[21]](cite://21/3). Local Government New Zealand expressed readiness to adapt, though its representatives acknowledged a 'tsunami of change' ahead for councils [[21]](cite://21/4). Environmental groups such as Forest & Bird have raised concerns about the pace of reform and potential erosion of environmental protections, particularly around freshwater [[22]](cite://22/1)[[15]](cite://15/5).

Would you like to explore a specific aspect of the reforms in more detail — for example, the freshwater protections, or how the Fast-track Approvals regime works?

4.document_title: Soil Erosion and Conservation in New Zealand: Comprehensive Analysis of Causes, Types, Management, and Control Methods
4.document_summary: This comprehensive document examines soil erosion and conservation in New Zealand from the 1940s to modern times. It explains that soil contains vital nutrients essential to farming and describes natural erosion processes including wind, rain, floods, and earthquakes. The document categorizes erosion into four main types: surface erosion (sheet and wind), fluvial erosion (rill and gully), mass-movement erosion (slips and earth flows), and streambank erosion. Human activities significantly accelerated erosion—settlers cleared forests and introduced grazing animals, exposing soil. By 1997, 50% of New Zealand experienced moderate to slight erosion, with 10% severe. New Zealand loses approximately 210 million tonnes of soil annually to rivers—about 10 times the global average. Hill country erosion costs $100-150 million annually, damaging infrastructure and aquatic ecosystems. The document traces management history from early surveys (Raeside and Gibbs, 1945) through key legislation including the Soil Conservation and Rivers Control Act (1941), Water and Soil Conservation Act (1967), and Resource Management Act (1991). Conservation methods implemented since the 1940s include tree planting, aerial topdressing, new farming techniques, and dam construction. Biological control methods include reforestation with poplars and pines, riparian strips, and shelter belts. Mechanical techniques include flumes, debris dams, bulldozing, and conservation tillage. Research demonstrates that reforestation successfully controls erosion while dense pasture reduces sheet erosion but cannot prevent slips and gullies.

6.document_title: Māori Land Rights, Indigenous Law, and Colonial Legislation in New Zealand: A Historical and Legal Analysis
6.document_summary:
This document examines the complex relationship between Māori traditional law and British colonial legislation in New Zealand from pre-Treaty times to 2011. It traces how Māori operated under a sophisticated customary law system based on concepts like mana, tapu, rahui, and utu before the Treaty of Waitangi (1840). Traditional Māori land rights were based on ahi kā (occupation) and various take (rights), contrasting sharply with colonial land laws that clashed with Māori communal land concepts.

The analysis documents systematic land dispossession through key colonial legislation including the Land Claims Ordinance 1841, Native Land Purchase Ordinance 1846, New Zealand Settlements Act 1863, and Native Lands Acts 1862-1865. The Native Land Court individualized Māori land titles to facilitate European settlement, causing severe hardship through distant hearings, high costs, and lengthy delays. The 1.3 million hectares confiscated under the Settlements Act exemplifies the scale of dispossession.

From the 1970s onward, Māori protests prompted significant legislative reforms recognizing customary rights and treaty principles. Key reforms include the Waitangi Tribunal (1975), Te Ture Whenua Māori Act 1993, Resource Management Act 1991, and landmark cases like Tom Te Weehi's 1986 fishing rights case. The document also addresses the intersection of Māori indigenous property rights with European marine law, demonstrating how Māori claims to traditional rights over marine areas are grounded in pre-existing legal traditions. By 2011, legislation increasingly incorporated Treaty of Waitangi principles and recognized Māori spiritual, cultural, and property rights.

7.document_title: New Zealand Estuaries: Comprehensive Guide to Ecosystems, Wildlife, and Conservation
7.document_summary: This comprehensive document explores New Zealand's estuaries, covering their formation, ecological characteristics, biodiversity, and conservation needs. Estuaries are coastal areas where fresh water mixes with sea water, forming unique and highly productive ecosystems. New Zealand has approximately 300 estuaries, with the largest being Kaipara Harbour at 15,000 hectares, formed about 6,500 years ago. These temporary landforms gradually fill with sediment, eventually becoming dry land. The document details diverse flora including seagrass (Zostera capricorni), mangroves (Avicennia marina), and salt marsh vegetation, as well as fauna such as mud worms, crabs, and cockles. Estuaries support at least 30 fish species and 17 native fish species that migrate between fresh and salt water, along with migratory birds from Siberia and Alaska. Historically important to Māori as food-gathering places and sacred sites, estuaries have been central to human settlement patterns. Major threats include silt accumulation, pollution, oil spills, invasive species, and sand extraction. The document emphasizes the importance of sustainable management under the Resource Management Act 1991, recognizing healthy estuaries as valuable natural assets that maintain coastal water quality, provide breeding grounds for numerous species, buffer against storms, filter pollutants, and offer recreational opportunities.

Regional councils throughout the country monitor water quality, and then decide how to manage land and effluent. 8.document_title: Water Quality in New Zealand: Comprehensive Assessment of Threats, Management Strategies, and Case Studies
8.document_summary: This comprehensive document examines water quality in New Zealand, addressing freshwater management and protection challenges. While New Zealand has high-quality freshwater by global standards, it faces significant threats from soil erosion, sewage, farm fertilizers, and algae growth. Major pollution sources include point sources (sewage pipes) and non-point sources (farm runoff), with contaminants encompassing sediments, organic matter, and dissolved chemicals like nitrate and phosphate. High nitrate levels pose particular health risks for infants. The document presents case studies of Lake Rotorua, Lake Taupō, and the Manawatū River, illustrating how human activities have degraded water quality. Management strategies outlined under the Resource Management Act 1991 include regional council monitoring, water-quality standards, and weed control methods. Key issues addressed include excessive nutrient levels causing algal blooms, invasive species like hornwort and didymo, and disease-causing organisms. Solutions involve multiple approaches: grass carp for vegetation control, restoring riparian shade, reducing nutrient inputs, improving farming practices, and implementing legislative protections. The document emphasizes voluntary farm management practices, including dairy farmer initiatives using effluent spraying and wetland treatment systems, a voluntary accord between Fonterra Co-operative Group and government entities to minimize dairying's environmental impact, and a Code of Practice for Fertiliser Use to mitigate agricultural harm.

21.document_title: Manapouri: New Zealand's Environmental Awakening - The Dam Controversy and Conservation Movement
21.document_summary: This comprehensive document chronicles the 50-year Manapouri hydroelectric controversy in New Zealand, from initial proposals in 1904 to the pivotal campaign of the 1960s-70s. The scheme involved raising Lake Manapouri's water level by 24-30 meters to generate hydroelectric power for an aluminium smelting operation by Comalco. Engineer Charles Turner championed the project as essential for New Zealand's industrial development, while conservationists like biologist John Salmon and the Forest and Bird Protection Society opposed it as environmental vandalism. The Manapouri power station, New Zealand's largest, was completed in 1969 at a cost of two billion dollars and 16 lives. Ecological research by Associate Professor Alan Mark revealed the delicate balance of lakeshore vegetation and consequences of water level manipulation. The Save Manapouri Campaign, led by Southland sheep farmer Ron McLean from 1969 onwards, became New Zealand's first nationally coordinated environmental movement, mobilizing over 250,000 petition signatures through innovative media strategies. Labour's 1972 election victory pledged to maintain the lake at natural levels, with Prime Minister Norman Kirk appointing six prominent campaigners as guardians to oversee lake management. This pivotal moment catalyzed significant legislative changes including the Resource Management Act and Official Information Act, inspired the formation of the Values Party and Greenpeace New Zealand, and marked a fundamental shift in New Zealand's environmental consciousness from resource exploitation to sustainable management.

[Page 1] Farmer productivity should improve under RMA reforms Federated Farmers ByGianina Schwanecke Producer/Presenter 2025 03 26 13:22:40+13:00 The government's proposed Resource Management Act (RMA) reforms will help improve farmer productivity by reducing red tape and compliance cost, according to Federated Farmers. RMA Reform Minister Chris Bishop unveiled details of the reforms at Monday's post Cabinet media conference, which include cutting red tape, boosting property rights, and removing the Treaty of Waitangi clause. Federated Farmers RMA reform spokesperson Mark Hooper said the current RMA was "broken", making it difficult to get things done with too many things requiring a resource consent. "Farmers are spending way too much time and money on costly resource consents and processes that are holding up investment in things like new water storage and rural infrastructure," he said. "The red tape and box ticking has become totally ridiculous." Hooper said there were a number of changes and a lot of detail still to be worked through, but the reforms were on the right track. He said the new framework which includes proposing two new acts, a Natural Environment Act and Planning Act will increase the number of permitted activities and reduce the number which require resource consent. "What seems to be the key theme is a shift from an effects based process to a focus on what's called externalities. And this is based around the principle of the enjoyment of property rights. "An externality is that if an effect doesn't have a negative impact on a third party beyond your property boundaries, then you should be free, within certain environmental limits, to do what you want." Hooper said the new laws will also mean that, where a council takes a property right away, the council will have to pay compensation for the loss of property value. "Federated Farmers has always pushed back on councils' overzealous use of overlays like Outstanding Natural Landscapes (ONLs), Significant Natural Areas (SNAs), or Sites and Areas of Significance to Māori (SASMs). "Farmers who've had a significant and unrelenting loss of property rights from restrictive overlays will be welcoming this news of a stricter regime. "Hopefully, under this new system, councils will be a lot more judicious about where they place an overlay and, when an overlay is used, the costs are sheeted home to those that receive the benefit." Federated Farmers also welcomed the shift to national standards, noting the Freshwater Farm Plan system is the ready to go standard for farming. Hooper said the model, introduced by the previous government and amended by the current, was a tool that can replace the need for a resource consent. "It is a ready to go standard for farming with huge buy in from farmers, sector groups, and regional councils." 35.text:
[Page 1] The big change to the Resource Management Act very little is known about ByFarah Hancock Data journalist, In Depth 2024 10 21 05:37:03+13:00 The coalition's very big law change that very little so far is known about The verdict on freshly announced plans for the replacement of resource management came in a swirl of words. Minister for Resource Management Reform and Infrastructure Chris Bishop and ACT's Simon Court had just delivered a speech to hundreds of resource management lawyers at their annual conference. The speech outlined changes to laws which control all manner of development, from massive infrastructure projects, to activities everyday New Zealanders might undertake on their properties. The crowd heard that the 900 pages of the current Resource Management Act (RMA), which attempts to balance development and the environment, will be thrown out, in favour of two new acts. When asked to give a one word reaction to the sweeping changes outlined in the speech, lawyers in the room typed their responses into the conference app. The words appeared on the big screen in a constantly refreshing word cloud. "Naive, was one of the big ones that came up," says Erika Tolman, Forest & Bird's acting general counsel, who attended the event. "Challenging" was another that made it to the screen, as was "ambitious". More positive responses were "opportunity", "promising" and "cautiously optimistic". One glowing response of "AMAZING" was given in all capital letters. These were tempered by less positive reactions. "Underwhelming", "misguided", "worrying", "ill conceived", "flip flop", "loose", "deja vu", "pessimistic", "vintage", "contradicting", "Toitū Te Tiriti", "inchoate" and "angry" also made appearances. The changes announced were significant and the pace to get them done, breakneck. The stated goal is to have the new acts in place before the next election rolls around in 2026. "I would say the time frames are very worrying, actually, because this stuff takes a long time. It needs proper thought put into it and rushing lawmaking, especially lawmaking that will affect us for generations and our environment for generations, is not a good idea," Tolman says. Changing the RMA is an idea which has had bipartisan support. Political parties have agreed that in its current form, it has failed to protect the environment enough, and at the same time wrapped projects up in excessive red tape. [flourish] 19821290 Bishop told conference attendees: "It's too hard to build a house. It's too hard to build roads, water and other infrastructure. It's too hard to secure the energy we need, including from renewables. High compliance costs have not always delivered the environmental outcomes we all want. The RMA protects the environment by resisting growth." New Zealand needs a system which protects the environment by setting limits that growth can occur within, Bishop said. The speech set out the third and final phase of changes. The completed phase one involved repealing two existing bits of legislation. Phase two involves significant tinkering by amending several bits of legislation and introducing the Fast track Approvals Bill. The third phase is the most ambitious, replacing the RMA with two new acts. One of these would likely be focused on development and the other on the environment. For lawyers listening to the speech, several questions remained unanswered. [flourish] 19857800 Tolman says the speech represented high level ideas, with "a lot of it based on anecdotes of worst case scenarios." "There are a lot of people scratching their heads and thinking how on earth is that going to work?" Enjoyment of property rights The guiding principle of the new resource management system is the "enjoyment of property rights". A fact sheet provided by Bishop's office explained this as allowing people to do more on their own property as long as it doesn't harm others. Environmental Defense Society CEO Gary Taylor is not convinced this is as simple as it sounds. "I'm not sure they know what property rights means yet. There are property rights individuals have. Arguably, there are property rights embedded in our environment. We have rivers that have property rights because they have legal personhood." Interpretation of the principle might differ depending on whether a narrow or wide view is taken. Taking a narrow view where individuals have rights to do whatever they want to on their land without concern for environmental effects would be a "disaster", he says. "That would be the unfettered right to do anything, our resource management laws need to be much more nuanced than that." Tolman is also unsure about how the guiding principle might work. She suspects it may be influenced by the backlash against Significant Natural Areas, or SNAs, where land owners who have significant areas of biodiversity on their land may be limited in what they can do in those areas, such as chop down trees without consent. "In a more urban space, what one person does on their property affects the next person's property values, for example, so I don't really know what they mean by that." Infrastructure New Zealand's policy director Michelle McCormick was not at the conference, but is closely following RMA reform for the industry association. She believes the starting premise of the enjoyment of property rights is people can do anything, until you "materially impact" someone else. New Zealand Planning Institute chair Andrea Harris was at the conference. The institute represents around 3000 planners, who grapple with the nitty gritty of implementing the RMA. She says the enjoyment of property rights is already a premise in the current RMA. While it's not the guiding principle, or purpose of the act, "it underpins it". National's Chris Bishop and ACT's Simon Court are leading work on replacements for the RMA Environmental bottom lines In Bishop's telling, protecting the environment will be achieved by setting environmental limits. He explained the second of the two replacement acts will do the job. "Quantified environmental limits, set by regional councils, should manage and control discharges for each environmental domain," he said. Simon Court continued the thread when he spoke: "There will be a 'double bottom line'," he said. "So councils will be required to provide for essential human needs such as housing, food production, drinking water and sanitation within environmental limits." He reiterated: "No environmental limit should make it impossible to building [sic] houses, produce food or energy, or provide transport. The right to housing and other essentials will be beyond question." Court's wording set off alarm bells for Tolman. "Basically you are saying that actually it's a limit, but not when it comes to those things." Taylor is in favour of environmental bottom lines, but says she is confused by Court's statement. "If by a double bottom line, they mean an overall, broad judgement, that is, we'll have a bottom line of development and a bottom line of environment, then that's going to be very confusing and is going to lead to a whole host of litigation." He doubts the double bottom line concept would "fly in the real world". McCormick is also unsure of how double bottom lines would work, but supportive of environmental limits. In order to have an impact, they "should be much more scientifically based". Planning disputes tribunal Bishop's speech suggested a tribunal be created to speedily resolve differences. "There will be rapid, low cost dispute resolution between neighbours, property owners, and councils embedded into the system. Further work will determine how best to achieve this, including the potential for a new Planning Tribunal, similar to the Disputes Tribunal, to resolve disputes quickly and affordably," Bishop told attendees. Tolman believes this idea relates to disputes between neighbours. "I'm not sure how it would work, but it's not a terrible idea if it's quicker, easier and more accessible for small disputes." However, she is concerned it could "denigrate" the role of the Environment Court. "There's quite a few hints in there that the Environment Court's role is going to be massively curtailed." Taylor sees merit in the idea of a tribunal but warns how that "radically new concept" would play out is unknown. McCormick says having a disputes tribunal could make justice more accessible and timely. "The experience currently with the Environment Court is quite a high hurdle and very costly to get there." A government legal aid fund of $600,000 for community groups to undertake environmental cases was cut in the 2024 budget. "It's probably become even harder to take a case there." Harris thinks there is merit in the idea, and sees it as a good place for disputes between neighbours to be dealt with. However, without more detail around how a tribunal would work, she says it is hard to formulate a proper opinion. [flourish] 19857837 Do we still need fast track legislation? "One stop shop" fast track legislation was part of the coalition agreement between National and NZ First. The reform of the RMA formed part of the National and ACT's coalition agreement. If the RMA reform is done well, is there any need to have both? Infrastructure NZ's McCormick doesn't think so. "I don't think you need both at all. This is an interim step to assist while we've got a very clogged up system at the moment," she says. "I would see the fast track [legislation] as a band aid solution at the moment." With the proposed changes to the way the RMA currently works in place she believes projects will be able to move faster. Tolman is also unsure. "The fast track does massively undermine the resource management system the way that it's drafted." In its current form, the fast track legislation is proposed to sit above and overrule the RMA, "so all the work that's being done to fix (so called) the RMA in the context of the fast track, is not going to have much effect," she says. Taylor's view is similar. "If we had good resource management law, you wouldn't need special purpose fast track legislation because that would be embedded somehow in the new law. Hopefully that will happen at some point." Harris is also sceptical. The only reason she sees for both to exist is that fast track legislation sits over several other pieces of legislation, such as the Wildlife and Conservation Acts. The need for speed The pace at which change will come worries both Tolman and Taylor. The panel assembled to create the blueprint for change is due to report back before Christmas, and legislation to be in place by mid 2026. "Frankly, I don't think they will get there," says Taylor, who describes the proposed timeline as "heroic" and "completely unrealistic" for something as big as the RMA. He describes the panel selected to create the blueprint as "surprisingly good", but faced with a monumental task in the time allowed. "I expect that's simply a way of putting pressure on everybody to do stuff, but there will be slippage. I think there has to be slippage because we can't afford to get this wrong." With several false starts on addressing issues with the current RMA, he would like to see change done in a way which will have bipartisan support. "We don't want to end up in 2027 with new law that the present government has put in place being repealed and replaced again by a new government. The whole point about this process is this is the second time round, and we've got to get it right. We can't keep doing this because it's so debilitating for both community groups, but also for our economic development and our environmental management." Harris also hopes the changes will get bipartisan support, and agrees the panel will need to work at pace. McCormick is excited work is underway, and that it appears to be a priority. When it comes to the timelines, she thinks anything is achievable if it is resourced properly. Ensuring there is enough time for engagement is critical, she says. The association supports the idea of two acts replacing the RMA, "but we need to really understand how they will work together". The result of the changes will impact everyday New Zealanders' futures, she says, and span from how communities are built, how transport is organised, where schools and businesses are located, and protect the environment. "I don't think there is any part of our lives every day that isn't touched and where planning decisions don't have an impact on it." [Page 1] Christopher Luxon reveals Resource Management Act reform ByRussell Palmer Political Reporter 2025 03 24 15:58:15+13:00 Chris Bishop the minister responsible for the reforms says the new approach could slash administrative and compliance costs by 45 percent. Prime Minister Christopher Luxon said the RMA was "the culture of 'no' that I spoke about earlier in the year brought to life". RMA Reform Minister Chris Bishop and Undersecretary Simon Court said replacing the RMA with law based on property rights would grow the economy and lift living standards. "The RMA is broken and everyone knows it. It makes it too hard to build the infrastructure and houses New Zealand desperately needs, too hard to use our abundant natural resources, and hasn't resulted in better management of our natural environment," Bishop said. "Cabinet has now agreed on the shape of the government's replacement legislation, signalling a radical transition to a far more liberal planning system with less red tape, premised on the enjoyment of property rights. He said the 45 percent estimated reduction in admin and compliance costs which was based on economic analysis of a "blueprint" developed by an Expert Advisory Group completed this year compared to a 7 percent reduction under Labour's proposed approach. Prime Minister Christopher Luxon. Several aspects of the reforms however appeared to closely resemble Labour's proposal. Like Labour's approach, it includes two new pieces of legislation a Natural Environment Act and a Planning Act and will streamline planning systems between councils, providing for more standardisation of consenting and increasing the number of "permitted" activities. It will also set environment limits, which the government's release said would provide more certainty around where development can and should be enabled, whilst protecting the environment just as Labour's proposed to do. He said he would be speaking to Labour and the Greens to see if there was some common ground, but noted it was government legislation and would be progressed in the form of the government's choosing. ByRussell Palmer Political Reporter, Giles Dexter Political Reporter 2025 12 09 19:22:28+13:00 Coalition reveals RMA replacement, but will it stand the test of time? 50.document_summary: The New Zealand government announced an expanded fast-track consenting regime to accelerate infrastructure projects. An expert panel will provide recommendations, with ministers making final decisions. Projects can be included in legislation or developers can apply directly to ministers. The system covers resource consents, marine consents, aquaculture decisions, and other approvals. Environmental protections remain in place through expert panel conditions. Some areas like reserves and customary Māori land are protected. The scheme prioritizes regionally and nationally significant projects such as roads, mining, and aquaculture. Ministers have broad powers to reject projects and can appeal panel conditions if deemed burdensome. Public hearings are not required, but consultation with local authorities and Māori groups is mandatory. The bill received Cabinet approval and first reading under urgency on March 7, 2024.

6.fileDescription: This comprehensive document explores New Zealand's estuaries, covering their formation, ecological characteristics, biodiversity, and conservation needs. Estuaries are coastal areas where fresh water mixes with sea water, forming unique and highly productive ecosystems. New Zealand has approximately 300 estuaries, with the largest being Kaipara Harbour at 15,000 hectares, formed about 6,500 years ago. These temporary landforms gradually fill with sediment, eventually becoming dry land. The document details diverse flora including seagrass (Zostera capricorni), mangroves (Avicennia marina), and salt marsh vegetation, as well as fauna such as mud worms, crabs, and cockles. Estuaries support at least 30 fish species and 17 native fish species that migrate between fresh and salt water, along with migratory birds from Siberia and Alaska. Historically important to Māori as food-gathering places and sacred sites, estuaries have been central to human settlement patterns. Major threats include silt accumulation, pollution, oil spills, invasive species, and sand extraction. The document emphasizes the importance of sustainable management under the Resource Management Act 1991, recognizing healthy estuaries as valuable natural assets that maintain coastal water quality, provide breeding grounds for numerous species, buffer against storms, filter pollutants, and offer recreational opportunities.

chunkHighlights.text: Since the passing of the Resource Management Act in 1991, local authorities have been required to manage estuaries and other coastal areas in a sustainable manner and respect Māori cultural and spiritual values.

7.fileDescription: This comprehensive document examines water quality in New Zealand, addressing freshwater management and protection challenges. While New Zealand has high-quality freshwater by global standards, it faces significant threats from soil erosion, sewage, farm fertilizers, and algae growth. Major pollution sources include point sources (sewage pipes) and non-point sources (farm runoff), with contaminants encompassing sediments, organic matter, and dissolved chemicals like nitrate and phosphate. High nitrate levels pose particular health risks for infants. The document presents case studies of Lake Rotorua, Lake Taupō, and the Manawatū River, illustrating how human activities have degraded water quality. Management strategies outlined under the Resource Management Act 1991 include regional council monitoring, water-quality standards, and weed control methods. Key issues addressed include excessive nutrient levels causing algal blooms, invasive species like hornwort and didymo, and disease-causing organisms. Solutions involve multiple approaches: grass carp for vegetation control, restoring riparian shade, reducing nutrient inputs, improving farming practices, and implementing legislative protections. The document emphasizes voluntary farm management practices, including dairy farmer initiatives using effluent spraying and wetland treatment systems, a voluntary accord between Fonterra Co-operative Group and government entities to minimize dairying's environmental impact, and a Code of Practice for Fertiliser Use to mitigate agricultural harm.

chunkHighlights.text: Water in New Zealand is protected by legislation, principally the Resource Management Act 1991. It provides a legal framework for using water, managing its quality, and balancing the needs of different groups
who affect or use water. For example, fishers and swimmers want the lakes and rivers to be clear, while factory owners need to dispose of waste material.

Regional councils throughout the country monitor water quality, and then decide how to manage land and effluent. In consultation with the local community, a council might decide to maintain high water quality in upland rivers and lakes for recreation and biodiversity, but allow some runoff and waste into lowland rivers and estuaries.

8.fileDescription: This comprehensive document examines soil erosion and conservation in New Zealand from the 1940s to modern times. It explains that soil contains vital nutrients essential to farming and describes natural erosion processes including wind, rain, floods, and earthquakes. The document categorizes erosion into four main types: surface erosion (sheet and wind), fluvial erosion (rill and gully), mass-movement erosion (slips and earth flows), and streambank erosion. Human activities significantly accelerated erosion—settlers cleared forests and introduced grazing animals, exposing soil. By 1997, 50% of New Zealand experienced moderate to slight erosion, with 10% severe. New Zealand loses approximately 210 million tonnes of soil annually to rivers—about 10 times the global average. Hill country erosion costs $100-150 million annually, damaging infrastructure and aquatic ecosystems. The document traces management history from early surveys (Raeside and Gibbs, 1945) through key legislation including the Soil Conservation and Rivers Control Act (1941), Water and Soil Conservation Act (1967), and Resource Management Act (1991). Conservation methods implemented since the 1940s include tree planting, aerial topdressing, new farming techniques, and dam construction. Biological control methods include reforestation with poplars and pines, riparian strips, and shelter belts. Mechanical techniques include flumes, debris dams, bulldozing, and conservation tillage. Research demonstrates that reforestation successfully controls erosion while dense pasture reduces sheet erosion but cannot prevent slips and gullies.

This document examines the complex relationship between Māori traditional law and British colonial legislation in New Zealand from pre-Treaty times to 2011. It traces how Māori operated under a sophisticated customary law system based on concepts like mana, tapu, rahui, and utu before the Treaty of Waitangi (1840). Traditional Māori land rights were based on ahi kā (occupation) and various take (rights), contrasting sharply with colonial land laws that clashed with Māori communal land concepts.

The analysis documents systematic land dispossession through key colonial legislation including the Land Claims Ordinance 1841, Native Land Purchase Ordinance 1846, New Zealand Settlements Act 1863, and Native Lands Acts 1862-1865. The Native Land Court individualized Māori land titles to facilitate European settlement, causing severe hardship through distant hearings, high costs, and lengthy delays. The 1.3 million hectares confiscated under the Settlements Act exemplifies the scale of dispossession.

From the 1970s onward, Māori protests prompted significant legislative reforms recognizing customary rights and treaty principles. Key reforms include the Waitangi Tribunal (1975), Te Ture Whenua Māori Act 1993, Resource Management Act 1991, and landmark cases like Tom Te Weehi's 1986 fishing rights case. The document also addresses the intersection of Māori indigenous property rights with European marine law, demonstrating how Māori claims to traditional rights over marine areas are grounded in pre-existing legal traditions. By 2011, legislation increasingly incorporated Treaty of Waitangi principles and recognized Māori spiritual, cultural, and property rights.

The new act explicitly recognised Māori spiritual and cultural values and the principles of the Treaty of Waitangi. Under this act, environmental developments required consultation with iwi , and applications for resource consents had to be sent to iwi authorities.

13.fileDescription: This article profiles Dr Jan Wright, New Zealand's Parliamentary Commissioner for the Environment, who serves as an institutional advocate for environmental protection. Wright, one year into her second five-year term, has actively opposed government attempts to weaken environmental safeguards. Key concerns include the 2012 Crown Minerals Act changes that gave the Minister of Energy and Resources equal say with the Minister of Conservation over mining on conservation land, and proposed Resource Management Act amendments that would introduce socioeconomic priorities and weaken environmental protections through vague language. Wright argues that "balance" between economic and environmental objectives represents a Trojan horse that distorts the RMA's purpose. She successfully opposed an Exclusive Economic Zone bill that would have prioritized economic benefits over environmental protection. Despite her advocacy role, Wright emphasizes her position is one of persuasion rather than enforcement, and warns that humanity has fundamentally overrun Earth's capacity.

chunkHighlights.text: This year, in a submission on proposed amendments to the Resource Management Act (RMA), Wright has made another blunt statement about the erosion of environmental safeguards. Seemingly anodyne changes that call for “balance” between economic and environmental objectives are, in the PCE’s view, a Trojan horse. “Balance of the kind where environmental and economic concerns are given equal weight does not belong inside the RMA,” she wrote.
“The RMA itself provides the balance to the economic imperatives of the marketplace. It is not, and should not become, an economic development act.”

Wright’s submission identified several areas of concern. Some involved subtle changes of wording that replace clear obligations with vague guidelines. For example, the act as its stands requires that public access to coasts and waterways be “maintained and enhanced”. The new wording merely says it ought to be “valued”—a concept open to interpretation. Elsewhere in the reforms, bedrock principles such as “ethic of stewardship”, “intrinsic value of ecosystems” and “maintenance and enhancement of amenity values” have been removed outright.

The most dangerous change, to the PCE’s mind, is the insertion of two socioeconomic priorities into the act: the provision of land for urban expansion and the provision of infrastructure. In cases where economic benefits and environmental costs are finely balanced, the presence of these objectives in the act would amount to an economic thumb on the scales. “The purpose of the act is being distorted,” says Wright.
The same strain of expediency showed up in 2011 in a bill governing the use of the Exclusive Economic Zone and the continental shelf. Wright opposed it there, too.

"There are a lot of people scratching their heads and thinking how on earth is that going to work?" Enjoyment of property rights The guiding principle of the new resource management system is the "enjoyment of property rights". A fact sheet provided by Bishop's office explained this as allowing people to do more on their own property as long as it doesn't harm others. Environmental Defense Society CEO Gary Taylor is not convinced this is as simple as it sounds. "I'm not sure they know what property rights means yet. There are property rights individuals have. Arguably, there are property rights embedded in our environment. We have rivers that have property rights because they have legal personhood." Interpretation of the principle might differ depending on whether a narrow or wide view is taken. Taking a narrow view where individuals have rights to do whatever they
want to on their land without concern for environmental effects would be
a "disaster", he says. "That would be the unfettered right to do anything,
our resource management laws need to be much more nuanced than
that." Tolman is also unsure about how the guiding principle might work.
She suspects it may be influenced by the backlash against Significant
Natural Areas, or SNAs, where land-owners who have significant areas of

biodiversity on their land may be limited in what they can do in those
areas, such as chop down trees without consent. "In a more urban space, what one person does on their property affects the next person's property values, for example, so I don't really know what they mean by that." Infrastructure New Zealand's policy director Michelle McCormick was not at the conference, but is closely following RMA reform for the industry association. She believes the starting premise of the enjoyment of property rights is people can do anything, until you "materially impact" someone else. New Zealand Planning Institute chair Andrea Harris was at the conference. The institute represents around 3000 planners, who grapple with the nitty-gritty of implementing the RMA. She says the enjoyment of property rights is already a premise in the current RMA. While it's not the guiding principle, or purpose of the act, "it underpins it". He explained the second of the two replacement acts will do the job. "Quantified environmental limits, set by regional councils, should manage and control discharges for each environmental domain," he said. Simon Court continued the thread when he spoke: "There will be a 'double-bottom line'," he said. "So councils will be required to provide for essential human needs such as housing, food production, drinking water and sanitation within environmental limits." He reiterated: "No environmental limit should make it impossible to building [sic] houses, produce food or energy, or provide transport. The right to housing and other essentials will be beyond question." Court's wording set off alarm bells for Tolman. "Basically you are saying that actually it's a limit, but not when it comes to those things." Taylor is in favour of environmental bottom lines, but says she is confused by Court's statement. "If by a double bottom line, they mean an overall, broad judgement, that is, we'll have a bottom line of development and a bottom line of environment, then that's going to
be very confusing and is going to lead to a whole host of litigation." He
doubts the double bottom line concept would "fly in the real world".
McCormick is also unsure of how double bottom lines would work, but
supportive of environmental limits. In order to have an impact, they
"should be much more scientifically based". Planning disputes tribunal
Bishop's speech suggested a tribunal be created to speedily resolve

differences. "There will be rapid, low-cost dispute resolution between
neighbours, property owners, and councils embedded into the system. Tolman believes this idea relates to disputes between neighbours. "I'm not sure how it would work, but it's not a terrible idea if it's quicker, easier and more accessible for small disputes." However, she is concerned it could "denigrate" the role of the Environment Court. "There's quite a few hints in there that the Environment Court's role is going to be massively curtailed." Taylor sees merit in the idea of a tribunal but warns how that "radically new concept" would play out is unknown. McCormick says having a disputes tribunal could make justice more accessible and timely. "The experience currently with the Environment Court is quite a high hurdle and very costly to get there." A government legal aid fund of $600,000 for community groups to undertake environmental cases was cut in the 2024 budget. "It's probably become even harder to take a case there." Harris thinks there is merit in the idea, and sees it as a good place for disputes between neighbours to be dealt with. However, without more detail around how a tribunal would work, she says it is hard to formulate a proper opinion. [flourish] 19857837 Do we still need fast-track legislation? "One-stop-shop" fast-track legislation was part of the coalition agreement between National and NZ First. The reform of the RMA formed part of the National and ACT's coalition agreement. If the RMA reform is done well, is there any need to have both? Infrastructure NZ's McCormick doesn't think so. "I don't think you need both at all. This is an interim step to assist while we've got a very clogged up system at the moment," she says. "I would see the fast-track [legislation] as a band-aid solution at the moment." 19.fileDescription: New Zealand's government announced plans to replace the Resource Management Act (RMA) with two new laws focused on private property rights and streamlined development processes. 20.fileDescription: Prime Minister Christopher Luxon announced the government's comprehensive Resource Management Act (RMA) reform plan. The new approach will replace the RMA with two Acts—a Natural Environment Act and a Planning Act—by end of 2025, with Select Committee review in 2026 and passage before the next election. The reforms aim to reduce administrative and compliance costs by 45%, compared to Labour's proposed 7% reduction. Key features include a shift to property rights-based planning, standardized zoning across councils (reducing 1,175 zone types to standardized categories), streamlined consenting processes, and increased "permitted" activities. The government will presume land uses are enabled unless they significantly impact others' property rights or the environment. Notable changes include removing the Treaty clause from current RMA requirements. Minister Chris Bishop criticized the current RMA as creating a "culture of 'no'" that hinders infrastructure and housing development, while the reforms aim to grow the economy and improve living standards.
